text: A lending pool's interest rate isn't set by a team typing in a number — it's computed from utilization, the fraction of supplied assets currently borrowed out. At 800,000 USDC borrowed out of 1,000,000 supplied, utilization is 80%. High utilization means little capital left for the next borrower, which should push rates up.

Almost every major lending protocol uses a kinked model: a gentle slope below a target utilization, then a much steeper slope above it. In an illustrative version, the rate rises gently from 0% to 4% as utilization climbs from 0 to 80%, then sharply from 4% up to 75% between 80% and 100%.

Run the numbers at three points: at 50% utilization, the borrow rate sits around 2.5%, comfortably on the gentle slope. At exactly 80%, the kink, it's 4%. At 95% — just fifteen points further — it's already around 42%. Same curve, wildly different behavior on either side of the kink.

Below the kink, the protocol wants borrowing cheap enough to attract demand, since idle liquidity earns suppliers nothing. Above it, the incentive flips hard — the protocol needs to discourage further borrowing and attract new supply immediately, because a pool at 100% utilization can't process withdrawals at all. The steep slope is a deliberate overcorrection, not a bug.

Suppliers don't earn the borrow rate directly. They earn a supply rate: the borrow rate scaled down by utilization itself, minus the protocol's reserve factor cut. At 80% utilization, a 4% borrow rate, and a 10% reserve factor, the supply rate works out to about 2.88%.
Borrowers pay the full rate on their debt; suppliers earn only a scaled share of it. Next: what actually happens when a borrower's health factor drops below 1.0, and who gets paid for stepping in.
